body:
How Can Corrosion Be Prevented?

Corrosion can often be slowed or prevented by reducing contact between a metal and harmful environmental substances, changing the metal's surface or selecting a material with greater corrosion resistance.

For iron and steel, an important objective is to reduce exposure to oxygen and moisture or provide additional electrochemical protection.

Barrier Protection: Painting, Oiling and Greasing

Paint, oil and grease act as protective barriers between the metal surface and the surrounding environment.

These barriers help prevent oxygen and water from contacting the metal.

  • Painting: Commonly used on steel gates, bridges, railings, structures and machinery.
  • Oiling: Useful for certain tools, moving parts and metal surfaces requiring temporary protection.
  • Greasing: Helps protect appropriate machine components against moisture while also providing lubrication.

Barrier protection depends on the continuity of the protective layer. If paint is scratched or peels away, the exposed iron may begin to rust.

Regular inspection and maintenance are therefore important for painted outdoor structures.

Galvanisation: Protecting Iron with Zinc

Galvanisation is the process of coating iron or steel with zinc to protect it against corrosion.

Zinc protects the underlying iron in 2 important ways.

  1. The zinc coating forms a barrier that reduces contact between iron and the environment.
  2. Because zinc is more reactive than iron, it can corrode preferentially and provide additional protection to the iron.

The second action is an example of sacrificial protection.

If a small area of galvanized steel becomes exposed, electrically connected zinc may continue to protect the iron nearby. This protection lasts only while sufficient zinc remains available.

Galvanisation is widely used for steel sheets, outdoor structural components, wires and other equipment that requires corrosion resistance.

Hot-dip galvanising commonly applies zinc by immersing prepared steel in molten zinc. Electro-galvanising uses electricity to deposit zinc. Therefore, galvanisation should not be treated as identical to electroplating in every situation.

Electroplating for Corrosion Protection

Electroplating can deposit protective metals such as chromium, nickel, tin or zinc on another metal surface.

The effectiveness of the coating depends on the coating material, thickness, adhesion, exposure conditions and whether the surface remains intact.

Some protective coatings primarily act as barriers. If such a coating is damaged, the underlying metal can become exposed to corrosive substances.

Anodising Aluminium

Aluminium naturally develops a thin aluminium oxide film when exposed to air. This film helps protect the underlying metal from further oxidation.

Anodising is an electrolytic process used to form a thicker protective oxide layer on aluminium.

During anodising, the aluminium article is made the anode in an electrolytic system. The process increases the thickness of its oxide coating, improving its resistance to corrosion and enabling certain surface finishes.

Electroplating deposits a different metal on a surface, whereas anodising aluminium primarily thickens the protective oxide layer of the aluminium itself. These are different surface-treatment processes.

Corrosion-Resistant Alloys

An alloy is a material formed by combining a metal with other elements to obtain desired properties.

Stainless steel is an important example of an iron-based alloy with enhanced corrosion resistance.

Chromium in stainless steel helps form a thin protective surface oxide film. Nickel may also be included in certain stainless-steel compositions to obtain desired properties.

Stainless steel is generally more resistant to ordinary atmospheric corrosion than unprotected carbon steel, although it is not completely immune to corrosion under every condition.

Comparing Common Protection Methods

MethodMain protective actionCommon example
PaintingCreates a barrier against moisture and oxygenSteel gates and bridges
Oiling or greasingReduces environmental contactTools and machine parts
GalvanisationZinc barrier and sacrificial protectionGalvanized steel sheets
ElectroplatingDeposits a desired protective metal coatingChromium-plated fittings
AnodisingThickens aluminium oxide coatingAluminium articles
AlloyingChanges material composition and propertiesStainless steel

Choosing an Appropriate Method

No single method is suitable for every metal or application. A painted steel railing, a galvanized steel sheet, an anodised aluminium component and a stainless-steel fitting rely on different protective mechanisms.

In humid or saline environments, the choice of material and coating must account for the exposure conditions. Protective coatings also require appropriate maintenance throughout their useful life.

Prelims focus

  • Galvanisation protects iron or steel using a zinc coating.
  • Zinc is more reactive than iron and can provide sacrificial protection.
  • Painting mainly works by separating the metal from oxygen and moisture.
  • Anodising thickens the protective oxide layer on aluminium.
  • Stainless steel obtains much of its corrosion resistance from chromium-containing protective surface films.
  • Trap: Galvanisation and electroplating are not identical processes; galvanisation specifically refers to zinc protection.

[NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 6, Physical and Chemical Changes, Section 6.3, Rusting of Iron, printed pp. 63–64, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 14, Chemical Effects of Electric Current, Section 14.3, Electroplating; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 3, Metals and Non-metals, Section 3.2.1 on anodising and Section 3.5.1 on prevention of corrosion, printed pp. 42 and 54, consulted textbook editions.]

body:
Why Electrochemical Technologies Matter

Batteries, electrolysis and corrosion protection are closely connected to energy supply, transportation and industrial development.

Batteries make electricity available when a generating source is unavailable or insufficient. Electrolysis uses electricity to manufacture useful substances. Corrosion prevention helps preserve the equipment and structures used in these activities.

Battery Energy Storage Systems

A Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) uses rechargeable batteries together with supporting electrical equipment to store energy and supply it when needed.

Solar and wind generation depend on changing environmental conditions. Electricity generated during periods of high renewable-energy production can be stored in suitable batteries and supplied later.

For example, a solar-powered installation may produce surplus electricity during daylight hours. A rechargeable battery can store part of this energy and supply electricity after sunset.

Battery storage can also support the electricity network by helping balance supply and demand and providing backup power. The amount of energy available depends on the installed battery capacity and operating conditions.

A solar panel generates electricity from sunlight, while a rechargeable battery stores energy through chemical changes. They perform different functions even when used together in one system.

India's Advanced Chemistry Cell Battery Programme

India approved the Production Linked Incentive Scheme for the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell Battery Storage on 12 May 2021.

The programme is administered by the Ministry of Heavy Industries and aims to encourage domestic manufacturing of advanced battery cells for applications such as electric vehicles and energy storage.

Important Programme Facts

  • Approval: 12 May 2021.
  • Implementing ministry: Ministry of Heavy Industries.
  • Approved financial outlay: ₹18,100 crore.
  • Manufacturing-capacity target: 50 GWh of Advanced Chemistry Cell battery storage.
  • Primary purpose: Strengthening domestic battery-cell manufacturing and reducing dependence on imported advanced cells.

Advanced Chemistry Cell is a broad programme category covering eligible advanced energy-storage technologies. It should not be confused with the name of one particular battery chemistry.

Implementation and Gujarat Connection

In its statement dated 21 July 2026, the Ministry of Heavy Industries reported that 40 GWh of the 50 GWh target had been awarded to beneficiary firms. The statement also listed a 5 GWh awarded project in Gujarat.

That statement reported cumulative investment of ₹5,180 crore through 31 May 2026. These figures describe the programme status reported for that period; awarded capacity and investment must not be interpreted as proof that the entire targeted manufacturing capacity was already operational.

These are dated implementation figures, rather than an assertion of further progress by the lesson's 3 November 2026 content cutoff.

National Green Hydrogen Mission

India's National Green Hydrogen Mission was approved by the Union Cabinet on 4 January 2023.

The mission supports the development of green hydrogen production, related technologies, domestic electrolyser manufacturing and industrial applications.

Its original approved financial outlay was ₹19,744 crore, and it targets the development of capacity to produce at least 5 million metric tonnes of green hydrogen annually by 2030.

Connection with Electrolysis

An electrolyser uses electrical energy to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. When suitable renewable electricity is used and applicable emissions conditions are satisfied, the resulting hydrogen can qualify as green hydrogen.

This links a basic chemical process studied at school level with modern industrial applications, including fertiliser production, petroleum refining and selected energy uses.

Gujarat's Deendayal Port and Green Hydrogen

Deendayal Port at Kandla, Gujarat, is one of the major ports recognised by the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy as a Green Hydrogen Hub under the National Green Hydrogen Mission.

The other recognised ports identified in the cited government updates are Paradip Port in Odisha and V. O. Chidambaranar Port in Tamil Nadu.

According to the Government of India's update dated 28 October 2026, a 1 MW green-hydrogen plant had been commissioned at Kandla Port in July 2025.

The project demonstrates the use of electrolysis in an industrial port environment. Its relevance to Gujarat is direct because the facility is located at Kandla.

Battery Storage and Hydrogen Production Are Different

Battery storage and electrolyser-based hydrogen production both use electricity but produce different immediate outcomes.

  • Rechargeable battery: Stores energy internally through reversible chemical changes and later supplies electricity.
  • Electrolyser: Consumes electricity to produce chemicals, such as hydrogen from water.
  • Hydrogen storage: Stores produced hydrogen as a chemical energy carrier for later use.

These technologies can support renewable-energy systems, but they are not interchangeable devices.

Responsible Management of Used Batteries

Used batteries can contain materials that should be recovered or handled separately from ordinary household waste. Recycling is important for recovering useful materials and reducing environmental risks.

India's Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, establish a framework for managing waste batteries and include Extended Producer Responsibility, under which producers have responsibilities related to collection, recycling or refurbishment.

Used lead-acid and lithium-ion batteries should enter appropriate collection and recycling systems. Lithium-ion batteries also require careful handling because damaged or improperly handled cells can present fire risks.

Responsible battery management therefore connects electrochemistry with resource conservation and environmental protection.

Connecting the Main Concepts

The principal relationship among the topics can be expressed through their energy transformations and applications.

  • Electrochemical cells: Chemical reactions can supply electrical energy.
  • Rechargeable batteries: Electrical energy can be stored through reversible chemical changes and released later.
  • Electrolysis: Electrical energy drives chemical reactions such as water decomposition and metal deposition.
  • Corrosion: Unwanted chemical or electrochemical reactions can damage metals.
  • Corrosion prevention: Protective coatings, suitable alloys and environmental control reduce metal deterioration.

Prelims focus

  • The Advanced Chemistry Cell Battery Storage PLI scheme was approved on 12 May 2021 with an outlay of ₹18,100 crore and a 50 GWh manufacturing target.
  • The programme is administered by the Ministry of Heavy Industries.
  • The National Green Hydrogen Mission was approved on 4 January 2023.
  • Deendayal Port at Kandla, Gujarat, is a recognised Green Hydrogen Hub.
  • The reported Kandla green-hydrogen plant has a capacity of 1 MW and was commissioned in July 2025.
  • Trap: A battery stores energy for later electrical use; an electrolyser consumes electricity to produce chemical substances.

[Press Information Bureau, Cabinet approval of the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell Battery Storage, 12 May 2021; Ministry of Heavy Industries, Press Information Bureau, PLI Scheme for Automobile and Auto Components and Battery Storage, 21 July 2026, implementation data through 31 May 2026; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, National Green Hydrogen Mission, January 2023, Sections 3–4 and 11; Press Information Bureau, Green Hydrogen: Emerging Pillar of India's Clean Energy Transition, 28 October 2026, sections on mission objectives and hydrogen hubs; Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Development of Green Ports and Maritime Infrastructure, 28 March 2026, Deendayal Port annexure; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, provisions on Extended Producer Responsibility and waste-battery handling; sources consulted 3 November 2026.]
